comments.subject: C: James Scott Skinner
comments.content: Strictly an air, for muted violin. Could play it for a strathspey dance though.    Original manuscript here: http://www.abdn.ac.uk/scottskinner/display.php?ID=JSS0577  Printed version here: http://www.abdn.ac.uk/scottskinner/display.php?ID=JSS0064  JSS plays it here: http://www.abdn.ac.uk/scottskinner/music/cd213a.m3u  And a YouTube version here: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=drM4STf1EiU

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: Setting 3 is the beautiful counterpoint written by Derek Hobbs and published in Book 3 of his series "Pipers Companion".

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: I'm shocked to see this presented as a reel. Scottish tunes get placed in some strange categories on here but this is possibly the strangest I've seen. It's The Cradle Song. A lullaby. A beautiful slow air. The suggestion of playing it as a Strathspey is also a bit bizarre!

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: Nessie, make yourself a nice cup of tea, sit down, calm down, breathe. There is no category for airs on this site, so we use workarounds to sneak them in. Your making a fuss might wake the giant and then the game will be up.  Anyway, when Niel Gow played "The Cradle Song" I'm sure he played it as a rather fast jig.    |A2c cBA|efe e2c|A2c cBA|B3 e2c|A2c cBA|efe e2d|cAE FAB|ABA A2:|

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: I'm sorry if this causes hurt and upset, but I've just imagined the conversation above as Nessie as Mrs. Pike and Nigel Gatherer as Wilson in Dad's Army!

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: That's what I was going for, Arabella. :-)

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: Others can argue whether this is an air or a reel.  What I find objectionable is that this, like many other Scottish tunes, is described as Irish on this site.      James Scott Skinner was a born in Aberdeenshire and wrote Cradle Song following an incident in Forres.

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: Where precisely is this tune described as "Irish" ?

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: Kenny, precisely, on entering Cradle Song on Google you get, for thesession.org, the description:  "A traditional Irish reel by James Scott Skinner with settings and ten comments that has been added to fifty-four tunebooks."  [Except now it'll probably be eleven comments.]    And read this comment from Phil Cunningham:  https://thesession.org/tunes/11698#comment970135

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: So the answer is "Google", not anyone at "thesession.org", so why bring it up here ? It wisnae us.

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: "What I find objectionable is that this, like many other Scottish tunes, is described as Irish on this site..."    David, David, David. Dinna fash. This is primarily a site for Irish music, but some awful Scots people have been sneaking in the odd ditty frae Caledonia, knowing that at ony moment they could be excommunicated. The site's benign leader Jeremy pretends tae be tolerant of this, but I hae witnessed him fuming, and shouting, "If we let the Scots in, what'll be next - Eng... Eng... THE ENGLISH?" So when you announce to all and sundry that a particular tune is Scottish, it just sets him off again, an' we dinna want that.     DonaldK, Kenny, myself and few other insurgents frae Alba meet clandestinely and carefully plan which tune we'll attempt to slip in through the back door next. By the way, I'm pretty sure that when Niel Gow played "The Cradle Song" he played it as a mazurka.

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: Well, there you go!  You shouldn't trust Google.  It says Niel Gow died in 1807 and James Scott Skinner, who wrote this traditional Irish reel, wasn't born till 1847.  Can't be true.  We know from Nigel that Gow played it both as a rather fast jig and as a mazurka.

comments.subject: Re: Cradle Song
comments.content: I think Nigel is getting mixed up. I don't think it was NIEL Gow but HARRY Gow who played The Cradle Song as a hornpipe, whilst waiting for his excellent steak pies to come out the oven.
